blocks.x: BIOL 151 · Cell Structure · Topic 4

From tiny oxidative microbodies to the cell's command centre and its internal scaffolding — this module covers the organelles that digest, control, and physically shape the eukaryotic cell, plus the diseases that result when they fail.

4types of microbodies: peroxisomes, glyoxysomes, hydrogenosomes, glycosomes ~60hydrolytic enzymes packed inside a single lysosome 3cytoskeletal filament types: microtubules, intermediate filaments, actin filaments
By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Describe microbodies and peroxisomes — their enzymes (urate oxidase, D-amino acid oxidase, catalase), their protective and metabolic roles, and how glyoxysomes and hydrogenosomes differ.

2Explain lysosome structure, formation and function — heterophagy, autophagy, autolysis, primary vs. secondary lysosomes, and the clinical consequences of lysosomal failure (silicosis, Tay-Sachs disease).
3Describe the nucleus and nucleolus — the nuclear envelope, pore/porosome structure, selective nuclear transport, chromatin organisation, and ribosome manufacture.
4Describe the centrosome and the three cytoskeletal filament systems — their structure, diameters, associated motor proteins, and functional roles in shape, transport and division.
5Connect cytoskeletal biology to medicine — Alzheimer's disease, cancer chemotherapy (Taxol, colchicine, vincristine), and intermediate filament diseases.

blocks.x: Key definitions

Microbody A heterogeneous group of small, vesicle-like organelles concerned largely with oxidation; usually oval or spherical and bounded by a single membrane. Found in the liver and kidneys of vertebrates, in the leaves and seeds of plants, and in protozoa, yeasts and other fungi.

Lysosome A membranous vesicle formed in the Golgi complex and filled with digestive (hydrolytic) enzymes. It pumps in H⁺ ions until its internal pH reaches about 5.0, the pH at which its enzymes are active.

Nucleus A large organelle bounded by a double-membrane nuclear envelope; the outer membrane is continuous with the rough ER. It houses the nucleolus, nucleoplasm and chromatin, and is perforated by water-filled nuclear pores.

Centrosome An organelle located near the nucleus containing the pericentriolar area, the site where the mitotic spindle and cytoplasmic microtubules form. Composed of two centrioles arranged at 90° to each other.

Cytoskeleton
A network of protein filaments and motor proteins in the cytoplasm that gives the cell shape and structural support, and enables movement of organelles, the whole cell, cilia, flagella, sperm, and chromosomes during division.
Microbodies & Peroxisomes→ Lysosomes & Clinical Disease→ Nucleus & Nucleolus→ Centrosome & Cytoskeleton Filaments→ Cytoskeleton in Disease & Medicine
Oxidative organelles

A family of small, single-membrane, vesicle-like organelles that specialise in oxidation reactions — detoxifying harmful substances, digesting purines and fats, and (in some anaerobes) releasing hydrogen gas.

Microbodies — the family Microbodies are a heterogeneous group of small, vesicle-like organelles concerned largely with oxidation. They are usually oval or spherical and bounded by a single membrane. They occur in the liver and kidneys of vertebrates, in the leaves and seeds of plants, and in protozoa, yeasts and other fungi. The family encompasses peroxisomes, glyoxysomes, hydrogenosomes and glycosomes.
Enzymes, purine catabolism & detoxification

Peroxisomes are membranous vesicles smaller than lysosomes. They form by division of pre-existing peroxisomes rather than budding from the Golgi. They participate in normal amino-acid and fatty-acid metabolism, and they oxidize toxic substances such as alcohol and formaldehyde. Their key enzymes are urate oxidase, D-amino acid oxidase, and catalase.

Urate oxidase — purine catabolism Converts urate into allantoin, CO₂ and H₂O₂ as part of purine catabolism. Peroxisomal enzymes are also involved in degrading L-α-hydroxy acids to oxoacids and H₂O₂, and oxoacids further on to acetyl CoA.

D-amino acid oxidase & catalase — protective function Gut bacteria break down proteins to release D-amino acids, which are toxic to the body. D-amino acid oxidase degrades these to oxoacids plus H₂O₂ — itself a toxic oxidizing agent. Catalase then rapidly degrades that H₂O₂ to harmless water and O₂, completing the detoxification pair.
Microbody types compared

c: Liver/kidney cells of vertebrates; most eukaryotic cells
Urate oxidase, D-amino acid oxidase & catalase reactions; detoxifies alcohol/formaldehyde; fatty-acid oxidation
Plant cells, especially germinating fat-storing seeds
Glyoxylate cycle converts stored fats to sugars for transport to growing tissue
Anaerobic eukaryotes — ciliates, trichomonads, some fungi & animals
Anaerobic energy generation, releasing molecular H₂ as a by-product

blocks.x: Turning fat reserves into sugar

Glyoxysomes are microbodies found in plant cells, where enzymes of the glyoxylate cycle predominate. Their job is to convert immobile fat reserves — for example, the oil stored in a germinating seed — into sugars that can be transported to growing tissues. Stored fats are first degraded to acetyl CoA, which feeds into the glyoxylate cycle to yield succinate. That succinate is then transported to the mitochondria, where it serves as a substrate for gluconeogenesis (sugar synthesis).
Stored fats→ Acetyl CoA→ Glyoxylate cycle→ Succinate→ Mitochondria (gluconeogenesis)
Hydrogen-producing organelles

Hydrogenosome A membrane-enclosed organelle found in the cytoplasm of some anaerobic eukaryotic cells — including ciliates, trichomonads, certain fungi, and some animals. It is named for its signature output: the release of molecular hydrogen (H₂) as a by-product of energy generation under anaerobic conditions.

blocks.title: Quick recap — microbodies at a glance

items: All microbodies share a single limiting membrane and an oxidative role.
Peroxisomes handle purine breakdown and detoxify H₂O₂ using catalase.
Glyoxysomes are the plant-seed fat-to-sugar converters via the glyoxylate cycle.
Hydrogenosomes are the anaerobic, H₂-releasing microbodies.
Peroxisomes multiply by dividing — they do not bud from the Golgi like lysosomes.

blocks.x: The cell's digestive system
Acidic, enzyme-packed vesicles that digest foreign material, recycle worn-out organelles, and — when they malfunction — underlie serious human diseases.

Lysosome — structural detail A lysosome has a single, smooth limiting membrane and contains roughly 60 hydrolytic enzymes (hydrolases) that are active at acid pH. An H⁺-ATPase in the lysosomal membrane pumps protons inward, lowering the internal pH to about 5.0 — the pH at which the hydrolases become active. The lysosomal membrane itself is resistant to its own hydrolases and impermeable to enzymes and substrates, but it is freely permeable to low-molecular-weight digestion products, which can diffuse out into the cytosol for reuse.
Heterophagy, autophagy & autolysis
Heterophagy
Digestion of foreign, extracellular material — e.g. bacteria or debris taken in by phagocytosis.
Autophagy
Recycling of the cell's own worn-out organelles — an intracellular process, e.g. digesting spent mitochondria or ribosomes.
Autolysis
Self-digestion of the cell after death, once the lysosomal membrane breaks down and releases its enzymes.
From Golgi to secondary lysosome

Primary lysosomes derive from coated vesicles released from the trans cisternae of the Golgi apparatus. Separately, receptor-mediated endocytosis delivers extracellular material into the cell inside an endosome. Fusion of that endosome with a primary lysosome produces a secondary lysosome. Phagosomes (phagocytic vesicles formed when the cell engulfs larger particles) can likewise fuse with primary lysosomes to give secondary lysosomes, which then digest their contents and release the absorbable products into the cytosol.
Golgi (trans cisternae)→ Primary Lysosome→ Fuses with Endosome / Phagosome→ Secondary Lysosome→ Digestion & Cytosolic Absorption

items: The lysosomal membrane houses an H⁺-ATPase that actively pumps protons into the lumen.
This drives the internal pH down to roughly 5.0, well below the neutral cytosolic pH.
Lysosomal hydrolases are acid hydrolases — optimally active only at this low pH.
If a lysosome ruptures, its enzymes are largely inactive at the neutral cytosolic pH, which limits (but does not eliminate) collateral damage.

blocks.x: Silicosis and related occupational lung disease

Silicosis Inhaled silica particles are taken up by phagocytes in the lung and liver. These particles rupture the lysosomal membrane, releasing digestive enzymes into the cytosol and killing the phagocyte. The resulting damage triggers fibroblasts to deposit collagen, which reduces lung elasticity and impairs breathing. Related occupational diseases follow the same basic mechanism with a different particle: asbestosis (asbestos fibres) and black lung disease (coal dust).
Lysosomal storage diseases & Tay-Sachs disease

When a specific lysosomal hydrolase is absent, its substrate accumulates inside cells instead of being broken down — a category of conditions called lysosomal storage diseases, with severe medical consequences.

Tay-Sachs disease A genetic disorder caused by the absence of a single lysosomal enzyme that normally breaks down a specific glycolipid in nerve cells. Without the enzyme, the glycolipid accumulates and causes progressive loss of nerve cell function. It disproportionately affects children of Eastern European (Ashkenazi Jewish) descent. Symptoms include seizures, muscle rigidity, blindness and dementia, with death typically occurring before age 5. Chromosome/carrier testing is now available to identify at-risk couples.

blocks.title: Compare the three lysosome-related disease mechanisms

items: Silicosis / asbestosis / black lung: an inhaled particle physically ruptures the lysosome, killing the phagocyte and triggering fibrosis.
Tay-Sachs disease: a missing enzyme means the substrate is never broken down, so it accumulates inside intact lysosomes and damages nerve cells.
Both categories show why the lysosome's dual role — as a digestive compartment and as a fragile, enzyme-rich sac — has direct medical consequences.

blocks.x: The cell's control centre
A double-membraned compartment that houses the genome, gates traffic in and out through selective pores, and manufactures the cell's ribosomes.

Nuclear envelope A double membrane separated by a perinuclear space. The outer membrane is continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum. The envelope is perforated by water-filled nuclear pores, which form where the outer and inner membranes fuse together.

The pore / annulus / porosome Each nuclear pore is surrounded by an "annulus" — eight protein granules arranged symmetrically around the opening. The pore together with its annulus is called a porosome. Glycoproteins within the porosome help regulate entry into the nucleus.

Selective nuclear transport Molecules larger than the pore itself can still pass through, provided they carry a signal sequence on the nuclear protein. This signal sequence enables the selective accumulation of specific proteins inside the nucleus, rather than allowing free diffusion of everything that fits.
Nucleoplasm & chromatin
The nucleus contains the nucleolus and the nucleoplasm. Embedded within the nucleoplasm are chromatin materials — the precursors of chromosomes.

Eukaryotic chromosome composition Roughly one-third DNA and two-thirds protein. Chromatin is the nucleoprotein complex formed from histones (small, basic proteins) plus non-histone proteins. Chromatin is organised into repeating structural units called nucleosomes. Humans have 46 chromosomes, and genes along them direct the synthesis of specific proteins.

c: Genes need to be accessible for transcription
DNA has already doubled and must condense for accurate segregation

blocks.x: Protein synthesis begins in the nucleus: DNA is transcribed into messenger RNA, which then leaves the nucleus and is translated into an amino-acid sequence that builds the protein.
DNA→ Transcription→ mRNA→ Translation→ Protein
Ribosome factory

Nucleolus A membrane-less organelle within the nucleus that manufactures ribosomes. It appears as a large, dark spot under the microscope. A given nucleus may contain up to 4 nucleoli — the exact number is fixed for a given species. The nucleolus reforms after cell division at specific nucleolar organizing regions on certain chromosomes, and it disappears during cell division.

Structurally, the nucleolus is composed of clusters of ribosomal genes surrounded by their own rRNA transcripts plus associated proteins. It is the site of rRNA synthesis and ribosomal-subunit assembly. There is also evidence of a possible link between nucleolus function and cellular aging / senescence.

items: The nuclear envelope is a double membrane continuous with the rough ER at its outer face.
Nuclear pores + annulus = the porosome; signal sequences allow selective, size-exceeding transport.
Chromatin = DNA + histone/non-histone protein, organised into nucleosomes.
The nucleolus builds ribosomes and disappears/reforms across the cell cycle.

blocks.x: Structure, transport & movement
A microtubule-organising centre near the nucleus, and the three filament families — with their motor proteins — that give the cell its shape and let it move things around.

Centrosome Located near the nucleus, the centrosome contains the pericentriolar area — the site of mitotic spindle and microtubule formation. It is composed of 2 centrioles positioned at 90° to each other, and each centriole contains 9 clusters of 3 microtubules (triplets) arranged in a ring. Centrioles replicate during cell division, and the centrosome also plays a role in cilia and flagella formation. Microtubules radiate outward from the centrosome toward the plasma membrane; the "plus" end — the end farthest from the centrosome — is where rapid lengthening and shortening occurs.
A dynamic, dual-purpose network

The cytoskeleton is a network of protein filaments and motor proteins that gives the cell its shape and structural support, and enables the movement of organelles, the whole cell, cilia, flagella, sperm, and chromosomes during muscle contraction and cell division. It has two broad roles:
Structural
Mechanical support, maintaining cell shape, and anchoring organelles in place.
Transport
Movement of molecules, organelles and cargo within the cell, and movement of the whole cell itself.

The cytoskeleton is dynamic: it can dismantle in one location and reassemble elsewhere to change the cell's shape. The classic example is the red blood cell's biconcave shape, which arises from its internal cytoskeleton.
The three filament types & their motor proteins

c: Cytoplasmic transport, axoneme movement, chromosome movement

blocks.x: Motor proteins Three key motor ("mover") proteins power cytoskeletal movement: kinesin and dynein, both associated with microtubules, and myosin, associated with actin filaments.
Hollow tubes built from tubulin

Microtubules are hollow tubes about 25 nm in diameter, of variable length, that are stiff yet flexible. They carry cargo along nerve axons that can exceed 1 metre in humans. They are built from tubulin dimers that polymerize end-to-end into protofilaments; 13 protofilaments arranged in parallel form the circular tube around a central lumen. Assembly requires the tubulin concentration to exceed a critical threshold. Tubulin subunits are polar — they have distinct "plus" and "minus" ends — and polymer growth proceeds from the plus end toward the minus end.

items: Centrosome = 2 centrioles at 90°, each with 9 triplets of microtubules; organises the mitotic spindle.
Microtubules (~25 nm, tubulin) pair with kinesin/dynein; intermediate filaments (~10 nm, keratin family) have no motor; actin filaments (~8 nm, actin) pair with myosin.
Microtubules are built from 13 protofilaments of tubulin dimers around a central lumen, and grow polarised, from plus end to minus end.
The cytoskeleton is structural (shape, support, anchoring) and transport-based (cargo and whole-cell movement), and it is dynamic — it remodels to reshape the cell.

blocks.x: When the scaffolding fails
Microtubule and intermediate-filament biology underlies Alzheimer's disease, several skin and liver conditions, and the mechanism of major anti-cancer drugs.
Alzheimer's disease

Tau protein & microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) MAPs, including tau protein, normally stabilize and stiffen microtubules. In Alzheimer's disease, microtubules are progressively lost from axons, while unorganised, tangled tau filaments accumulate instead. This impairs axonal transport and leads to loss of nerve-cell function. The exact underlying cause of this shift is not yet fully understood.
Targeting the mitotic spindle in cancer chemotherapy

Cancer is fundamentally a disease of uncontrolled cell division. Because the mitotic spindle's microtubules must continually grow and shrink to align and separate chromosomes, they are a prime drug target. There are two opposing strategies:
Disrupt assembly blocks polymerisation
Prevents microtubules from polymerising in the first place, so the spindle cannot form and division halts.
Lock/stabilize assembly prevents disassembly
Freezes already-assembled microtubules in place so they can no longer shrink, again blocking division.
Taxol Inhibits microtubule disassembly, locking microtubules static so the spindle can no longer function — this blocks cell division from the "stabilizing" side of the strategy.

Colchicine, nocodazole & vincristine Inhibit microtubule assembly — they block polymerisation and promote depolymerisation, preventing the spindle from forming. Vincristine is used clinically in cancer chemotherapy.

c: Inhibits microtubule assembly; used in cancer chemotherapy

blocks.x: Three conditions linked to intermediate filaments
Epidermolysis bullosa simplex A skin-blistering disease caused by the lack of normal keratin filament bundles, leaving skin cells unable to withstand mechanical stress.

Alzheimer's disease (neurofilament changes) A separate mechanism from the tau/microtubule pathway above: Alzheimer's disease is also associated with changes in neurofilaments, a class of intermediate filament found in neurons.
Alcoholic liver cirrhosis Involves the accumulation of keratin filaments in liver cells, forming aggregates known as Mallory bodies.
The fluid the cytoskeleton sits in

Cytosol Makes up about 55% of cell volume and is roughly 75–90% water plus other components. Large organic molecules — proteins, carbohydrates, lipids — are suspended by electrical charges, while small organic molecules (simple sugars) and ions are simply dissolved. Large aggregates such as lipid droplets and glycogen granules are called inclusions. The cytosol is the site of many important reactions, including ATP production and the synthesis of building blocks such as amino acids.

items: Alzheimer's has two distinct cytoskeletal links: tangled tau destabilizing microtubules, and separately, changes in neurofilaments (intermediate filaments).
Taxol stabilizes/locks microtubules (blocks disassembly); colchicine, nocodazole and vincristine block assembly (polymerisation) — both strategies halt mitosis.
Vincristine is the one of this group in clinical cancer chemotherapy use.
Epidermolysis bullosa simplex (missing keratin bundles) and alcoholic cirrhosis (Mallory bodies from keratin accumulation) are both intermediate-filament diseases.
The cytosol — mostly water — is the fluid medium in which the whole cytoskeleton and organelles are suspended, and where ATP production and amino-acid synthesis occur.
